newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn sticks by goal of halving jobless - Kohl.
newsitem.headline: Bonn sticks by goal of halving jobless - Kohl.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Sunday the German government stood by its goal of halving unemployment by the year 2000.

Many leaders in industry and unions, and even members of Kohl's own cabinet, have publicly abandoned the effort since it was launched a year ago, as unemployment rose to its highest level since the 1930s Depression, easing back only with the seasonal thaw in February and March.

"Instead of speculating about whether the goal is reachable, everything should be undertaken to make progress in that direction," Kohl said at the opening of the Hanover Industry Trade Fair, according to a prepared summary of his speech.

Reform of the tax and social security systems, cuts in non-wage labour costs and investment incentives for the construction industry were all initiatives the government was undertaking to reduce unemployment, Kohl said.
He said the economic outlook was positive and improving as a seasonal spring recovery begins. Unadjusted unemployment declined by 190,000 in March, but remained unacceptably high at 4.48 million.
"The most important task is to improve the conditions for new jobs," Kohl said.

He added that European monetary union was a central building block for the continued integration of Europe. "The convergence criteria for EMU are not open to negotiation, and the timetable is also important," he said.
The annual Hanover Fair remains the world's largest industrial trade fair, with a record 7,259 exhibitors this year, ranging from automation and lighting to warehouse equipment and plant engineering.
Rail technology will be a special focus of this year's fair, with France's SNCF showing its next-generation "Thalys" high-speed train.
Major exhibitors include titans of German industry such as engineering group Siemens AG and steel maker Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp, but also thousands of small and mid-sized companies.
Britain, this year's "Partner country", is represented by British Aerospace, Rolls-Royce and others.
Some 300,000 visitors are expected at the fair this year, bringing three billion marks ($1.7 billion) in revenue to the Hanover economy, and creating 17,000 jobs in this unemployment-sensitive era.

While Germany remains a more traditionally industrial, coal-and-steel nation than the United States or Britain, the Hanover Industry Fair has for years been eclipsed by its offspring, the Cebit computer fair, which takes place each year at the same location.
Cebit attracts a similar number of exhibitors, but far more visitors, and generates more revenue for Deutsche Messe AG, the company that administers both fairs.
Deutsche Messe AG is aiming to attract 300,000 visitors each day to the Expo 2000 World's Fair, which will also take place here.

This year marks the 50th anniversary of the Hanover Trade Fair. Britain was chosen as the partner country because it also played a major role in the very first Hanover fair in 1947, as an occupied Germany was rebuilding from the destruction of World War Two.

"This anniversary fair is symbolic of the immensely successful partnership in innovation and trade between Britain and Germany," Prince Philip, husband of Britain's Queen Elizabeth, said at the opening ceremony.
Germany is Britain's largest export market, and each is the other's largest foreign investor, he noted.
